```{r setup, include=FALSE}

#   warning = FALSE -> hide warnings

```

# Part 1 · RStudio Projects and R Markdown

An **RStudio Project** is a folder with an `.Rproj` file. Opening the `.Rproj` file sets the working directory to that folder. All paths in our code are **relative** to the project root, so the code runs on every laptop.

When you knit, R runs the document in the folder of the `.Rmd` file (`session_01/`). The **here** package always finds the project root (the folder containing the `.Rproj` file) — regardless of where the document lives.

### Chunk 1.1 · Where am I?

```{r chunk_1_1}
## Where does R look for files right now?
getwd()
```

### Chunk 1.2 · Relative paths with here()

```{r chunk_1_2}
## Install once (Console!): install.packages("here")

## Load the package (needed in every session)
library(here)

## The project root
here()

## Build a path to the data folder — works on Windows, Mac and Linux
here("data", "compustat.csv")

## Does the file exist? (TRUE once you have copied the Moodle files into data/)
file.exists(here("data", "compustat.csv"))
```

Compare this with an **absolute path** such as `"C:/Users/seitz/Documents/01_Lehre/compustat.csv"` — it only works on my laptop. Note also: R wants forward slashes `/` (or doubled backslashes `\\`) in paths.

### Exercise 1.3 · Make the document yours

1.  Replace the author in the YAML header at the very top with your name.
2.  Knit the document (`Ctrl+Shift+K`). An HTML file appears next to the `.Rmd`.
3.  Try the **Visual** editor (button top left of the editor) and switch back to **Source**.

Visual is always available, before or after knitting. It’s just another way to edit your .Rmd. Code results are not computed there.
Knitting creates a separate HTML file (Session_01_student.html, next to your .Rmd).

**Markdown reminder:** `# Heading`, `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `- bullet`, `[link](https://www.lmu.de)`, inline formula `$\beta_1$`, block formula `$$y = a + b x$$`.

# Part 2 · Git and GitHub

Git = program on your laptop that saves snapshots (commits) of your project folder, so you have a full history instead of many file copies.
GitHub = website that stores your project and its history online (backup + sharing).
Why in this course: to get the course material from Dr. Seitz, save your work with a history, and hand it in.
Pull = download newest version from GitHub.
Work = edit your files.
Commit = save a snapshot on your laptop.
Push = upload your snapshots to GitHub.
eval = FALSE = these chunks don’t run when knitting; you run them once yourself in the Console (one-time setup).

### Chunk 2.1 · Is Git installed and does RStudio find it?

```{r chunk_2_1, eval=FALSE}
## Install the helper packages once: When installing packages, write into console
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))

## Health report of your Git/GitHub setup
usethis::git_sitrep()
##Very good news: this is a healthy report. You must have set this up before, because almost everything is already done:
```

If Git is missing: **Windows** — install from <https://git-scm.com> (defaults are fine). **Mac** — run `xcode-select --install` in the Terminal. Then check *Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN* and restart RStudio.

### Chunk 2.2 · Tell Git who you are

```{r chunk_2_2, eval=FALSE}
## Use the e-mail address of your GitHub account
usethis::use_git_config(user.name  = "Jane Doe",
                        user.email = "jane.doe@campus.lmu.de")
```

### Chunk 2.3 · Give RStudio a key to GitHub (personal access token)

```{r chunk_2_3, eval=FALSE}
## Opens github.com in the browser with sensible defaults.
## Set an expiry date (e.g., end of March 2027) and click "Generate token".
usethis::create_github_token()

## Paste the token when asked. Never put the token into a script or commit it!
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()

## Check again — everything should be fine now
usethis::git_sitrep()
```

### Exercise 2.4 · Fork and clone the course repository

On **github.com**:

1.  Open the course repository (link on the room screen, in the Zoom chat and on Moodle).
2.  Click **Fork → Create fork**. You now own a copy: `github.com/YOUR-NAME/EmpRes-Tutorial`.
3.  In *your fork*, click the green **\<\> Code** button and copy the HTTPS URL.

Explanation:
Repository (repo) = a project folder with its full history, stored on GitHub
Fork = your own copy of someone else’s repo on GitHub (yours: Alex-M-lmu/Empirical_Research_WS26)
Commit = a saved snapshot with a short message (e.g. “Name edit”)
Ahead / behind = how many commits you have that the original doesn’t, and vice versa
Sync fork = pulls new material from Dr. Seitz’s original into your fork
Clone = downloads your fork from GitHub to your laptop (once)
Pull = downloads new changes from GitHub to your laptop
Push = uploads your new commits from your laptop to GitHub
Public = everyone can see it, so never upload licensed data, personal data or tokens

In **RStudio**:

4.  *File → New Project → Version Control → Git*, paste the URL.
5.  Choose a parent folder **outside** OneDrive/Dropbox/iCloud (cloud sync and Git do not get along).
6.  *Create Project*. RStudio opens `EmpRes-Tutorial.Rproj`, the **Git** tab appears top right.
7.  Copy `compustat.csv` and `compustat_German_format.csv` from Moodle into the `data/` folder. They will **not** be uploaded to GitHub (see `.gitignore`): Compustat is licensed data.

**Getting my new material later:** on github.com open your fork → **Sync fork → Update branch**, then click **Pull** (blue arrow) in RStudio.

# Part 3 · R basics

## R as a calculator

Basic operations: `+ - * / ^`. Some functions:

| Description          | R code        |
|----------------------|---------------|
| Absolute value       | `abs(x)`      |
| Square root          | `sqrt(x)`     |
| Exponential function | `exp(x)`      |
| Natural logarithm    | `log(x)`      |
| Round to s digits    | `round(x, s)` |

The assignment operator is the arrow `<-` (shortcut `Alt + -`). `=` also works but is not recommended. `#` starts a comment. R is **case-sensitive**.

### Chunk 3.1 · Calculator and assignment

```{r chunk_3_1}
## Assign values to objects (no output)
1 + 1
5 * (4 - 1)^2
sqrt(log(10))      # functions can be nested: first log(10), then the square root

## Fun with floating point: Euler's identity e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0
## Assign values to objects (no output)
x <- 5             # "x gets 5": stored in memory, appears in the Environment pane
X <- 6             # different object! R is case-sensitive (x ≠ X)
x^2                # use the object in a calculation

## Lesson: never test numbers with == after calculations, use all.equal()
## Fun with floating point: Euler's identity e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0
exp(1i * pi) + 1   # should be exactly 0, but R shows a tiny rounding error (~1e-16)
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3   # FALSE! Same problem: computers store decimals only approximately

```

## Objects and data types

R works with objects: numbers, text, vectors, matrices, data frames, functions, results … The main data types are **numeric**, **character** (text), **logical** (TRUE/FALSE) and **integer**. `class()` tells you the type, `as.numeric()`, `as.character()` etc. convert. The decimal separator is a **point**. `rm()` deletes an object.

### Chunk 3.2 · Data types

```{r chunk_3_2}
## Data types: class() tells you what type an object is
class(42)          # "numeric"   = number
class("Munich")    # "character" = text (always in quotes)
class(TRUE)        # "logical"   = TRUE / FALSE
class(42L)         # "integer"   = whole number (the L makes it integer)

## Conversion
as.character(42)   # number -> text: "42"
as.numeric("42")   # text -> number: 42
as.numeric("Munich")   # text that isn't a number -> NA (= missing value)
as.numeric("001004")   # -> 1004: leading zeros are lost!

## Delete an object
y <- 10            # create an object (appears in the Environment)
rm(y)              # delete it (disappears from the Environment)

```

### Chunk 3.3 · Logical operators

| Description              | R code   |
|--------------------------|----------|
| Equal to                 | `x == y` |
| Less than                | `x < y`  |
| Greater than or equal to | `x >= y` |
| Not equal to             | `x != y` |
| Not                      | `!b`     |
| Or                       | `a | b`  |
| And                      | `a & b`  |

```{r chunk_3_3}
## Logical operators: every comparison returns TRUE or FALSE
x <- 5
y <- 3

x == y        # equal to?                 FALSE
x < y         # less than?                FALSE
x >= y        # greater than or equal?    TRUE
x != y        # not equal?                TRUE

## Combine conditions
a <- x > 4    # TRUE
b <- y > 4    # FALSE

!b            # not:  turns FALSE into TRUE
a | b         # or:   TRUE if at least one is TRUE  -> TRUE
a & b         # and:  TRUE only if both are TRUE    -> FALSE

## Common mistake: = assigns, == compares
x == 3        # asks "is x 3?"  -> FALSE


```

# Part 4 · Our student cities

**Welcome to our running example: you!**

Before we work with real accounting data, we practise with data we all know: the universities and cities where you study. Because you know these data, you will notice immediately when your code produces something wrong.

| Students | University                    | City      |
|---------:|-------------------------------|-----------|
|        8 | LMU Munich                    | Munich    |
|        1 | Aalto University              | Espoo     |
|        1 | Stockholm School of Economics | Stockholm |
|        1 | University of Mannheim        | Mannheim  |
|        1 | University of Eastern Finland | Joensuu   |
|       +1 | exchange / second city        | Vienna    |
|       +1 | exchange / second city        | Shanghai  |

And this is what we know about the cities:

| City | Country | Inhabitants (approx.) | At the sea? | Party drink | Alcohol-free |
|------------|------------|-----------:|------------|-------------|------------|
| Munich | Germany | 1,510,000 | no | Helles beer | Spezi |
| Espoo | Finland | 320,000 | yes | Lonkero | Jaffa |
| Stockholm | Sweden | 990,000 | yes | Akvavit | Julmust |
| Mannheim | Germany | 315,000 | no | Riesling Schorle | Apfelschorle |
| Joensuu | Finland | 78,000 | no | Koskenkorva | Kotikalja |
| Vienna | Austria | 2,000,000 | no | Spritzer | Almdudler |
| Shanghai | China | 24,900,000 | yes | Huangjiu | Suanmeitang |

*Note:* The population numbers below were drafted with the help of AI and rounded. Are they right? That is Task A2.

## Vectors

The simplest way to collect many values is a **vector**: `c(value1, value2, ...)`. A vector has **exactly one data type**.

| Description                   | R code                         |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Number of elements            | `length(x)`                    |
| Largest / smallest value      | `max(x)`, `min(x)`             |
| Sort                          | `sort(x)`                      |
| Sum / product / mean          | `sum(x)`, `prod(x)`, `mean(x)` |
| n copies of z                 | `rep(z, n)`                    |
| Sequence from f to t (step s) | `seq(f, t, s)` or `f:t`        |

### Chunk 4.1 · Create vectors

```{r chunk_4_1}
## Create vectors: c() = "combine" several values into one vector
cities <- c("Munich", "Espoo", "Stockholm",
            "Mannheim", "Joensuu", "Vienna", "Shanghai")
inhabitants <- c(1510000, 320000, 990000,
                 315000, 78000, 2000000, 24900000)

## Give the elements names
names(inhabitants) <- cities   # each number gets its city as a label
inhabitants

## Vector functions
length(cities)          # number of elements: 7
sum(inhabitants)        # total inhabitants
mean(inhabitants)       # average
max(inhabitants)        # largest value
min(inhabitants)        # smallest value
sort(inhabitants)       # sorted from small to large

## Special vectors
1:10                    # sequence 1, 2, ..., 10
seq(1, 10, 2)           # from 1 to 10 in steps of 2: 1 3 5 7 9
rep("beer", 3)          # "beer" three times

## Calculations work element by element
inhabitants / 1e6       # every city in millions (1e6 = 1,000,000)
sum(inhabitants) / 1e6  # total in millions
```

### Chunk 4.2 · Indexing

```{r chunk_4_2}
## Indexing = picking elements out of a vector with [ ]

## By position (R starts counting at 1, not 0)
cities[1]                  # first element: "Munich"
cities[c(2, 3)]            # second and third element
cities[-1]                 # all EXCEPT the first

## By name (works because we gave inhabitants names)
inhabitants["Vienna"]
inhabitants[c("Munich", "Mannheim")]

## By condition: TRUE/FALSE for each element, keep the TRUE ones
inhabitants > 1e6                  # check: which cities have more than 1 million?
inhabitants[inhabitants > 1e6]     # keep only those

```

**Task A1:** Which of "your" cities have more than 1 million inhabitants? How many are they?

```{r task_A1}
## Which cities have more than 1 million inhabitants?
big <- inhabitants[inhabitants > 1e6]   # keep only cities with > 1 million
names(big)                              # their names

## How many are they?
length(big)                             # count the elements
sum(inhabitants > 1e6)                  # alternative: TRUE counts as 1, FALSE as 0

## Check with what we know: Munich (1.51 m), Vienna (2.0 m), Shanghai (24.9 m) -> 3

```

**Task A2 (verification):** Look up the population of *one* city in an official source (e.g., the statistical office of the country). Is our rounded number close enough? What exactly is counted — city proper or metropolitan area?
- Our number (1,510,000) matches the official state/federal figure for the city proper (about 1.51 million, 2024).
- The city's own statistical office reports more, because it counts from the residents' register instead of the census.
- Lesson: a plausible number isn't enough, always check what is measured and by whom.
  
## Factors

A **factor** maps labels to an underlying integer code. Factors are useful for categories such as countries, industries or audit firms.

### Chunk 4.3 · Factors

```{r chunk_4_3}
## Factor = category variable: labels stored with an integer code behind them
country <- factor(c("Germany", "Finland", "Sweden",
                    "Germany", "Finland", "Austria", "China"))
country

## The categories (levels), sorted alphabetically
levels(country)

## How often does each category occur?
table(country)

## Behind the scenes: each label is a number (its position in levels)
as.integer(country)

```

## Matrices — and the matrix trap

`cbind()` combines vectors column-wise, `rbind()` row-wise. Like a vector, a **matrix has exactly one data type**.

### Chunk 4.4 · Matrices

```{r chunk_4_4}
## Create a matrix: cbind() puts vectors side by side as columns
m <- cbind(inhabitants, students = c(8, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1))
m                              # rows = cities (from the names), columns = inhabitants, students
class(m[, "inhabitants"])      # "numeric": everything is still a number

## Add a text column: is the city at the sea?
m2 <- cbind(m, sea = c("NO", "YES", "YES", "NO", "NO", "NO", "YES"))
m2                             # look closely: now ALL values have quotes -> all text!

## Add a row: rbind() adds a row at the bottom (UEF's second campus, approx. inhabitants)
m3 <- rbind(m2, Kuopio = c(124000, 0, "NO"))
m3

## Indexing: first row, then column  -> m[row, column]
m2["Munich", ]                 # one row: everything about Munich
m2[, "sea"]                    # one column: sea for all cities
m2[1, 2]                       # row 1, column 2: Munich's students
```

**Task B:** Run `sum(m2[, "inhabitants"])`. What happens and why? How could you have noticed **before** the error?

```{r task_B, error=TRUE}
## error=TRUE: show the error in the HTML and keep knitting

## What happens?
sum(m2[, "inhabitants"])        # Error: invalid 'type' (character) of argument

## Why? The column is text, not numbers
class(m2[, "inhabitants"])      # "character"

## How could I have noticed BEFORE the error?
class(m[, "inhabitants"])       # "numeric" -> fine before the text column was added
str(m2)                         # chr = character for the whole matrix

## Fix 1: convert back to numbers
sum(as.numeric(m2[, "inhabitants"]))

## Fix 2 (better): keep mixed types in a data frame (Chunk 4.6)

```

## Lists

A **list** is a bag that can hold any objects of any length and type.

### Chunk 4.5 · Lists

```{r chunk_4_5}
## A list can hold objects of different types AND lengths
party <- list(title  = "Course party",                       # one text
              cities = cities,                               # vector of 7 texts
              drinks = c(Munich    = "Helles beer",
                         Espoo     = "Lonkero",
                         Stockholm = "Akvavit",
                         Mannheim  = "Riesling Schorle",
                         Joensuu   = "Koskenkorva",
                         Vienna    = "Spritzer",
                         Shanghai  = "Huangjiu"),            # named vector of 7 texts
              guests = 14)                                   # one number
str(party)                     # overview: what is in the bag?

## Access elements with $
party$title
party$drinks["Munich"]         # first $ to get the drinks, then [ ] to pick one

```

## Data frames

A **data frame** is the most important object for data analysis: a rectangle with **columns = variables** and **rows = observations**. Each column has one type, but different columns can have different types. **Tidy data:** every column a variable, every row an observation, every cell a single value.

Useful functions: `data.frame()`, `head()`, `str()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()`, `summary()`, `subset()`, `df$column`.

### Chunk 4.6 · Data frames

```{r chunk_4_6}
## One row per city
df_cities <- data.frame(
  city        = cities,                                           # character
  country     = country,                                          # factor
  inhabitants = inhabitants,                                      # numeric
  at_sea      = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE),  # logical
  drink       = c("Helles beer", "Lonkero", "Akvavit", "Riesling Schorle",
                  "Koskenkorva", "Spritzer", "Huangjiu"),         # character
  drink_free  = c("Spezi", "Jaffa", "Julmust", "Apfelschorle",
                  "Kotikalja", "Almdudler", "Suanmeitang")        # character
)

## Look at it
df_cities
str(df_cities)                 # one type per column - no matrix trap!
nrow(df_cities)                # number of rows (cities)
ncol(df_cities)                # number of columns (variables)
summary(df_cities)             # quick overview of every column

## Work with it
df_cities$inhabitants                       # one column with $
sum(df_cities$inhabitants)                  # works: the column stayed numeric
subset(df_cities, inhabitants < 1e6)        # only cities below 1 million

```

The student data are given — run this chunk:

```{r students_data}
## One row per student (given, anonymous IDs, home university)
students <- data.frame(
  student_id = sprintf("S%02d", 1:12),
  university = c("LMU", "LMU", "LMU", "LMU", "LMU", "LMU", "LMU", "LMU",
                 "Aalto", "SSE", "Mannheim", "UEF"),
  city       = c("Munich", "Munich", "Munich", "Munich", "Munich", "Munich",
                 "Munich", "Munich", "Espoo", "Stockholm", "Mannheim", "Joensuu")
)
```

```{r chunk_4_6b}
## Explore the students data
## Explore the students data
head(students)                 # first 6 rows
str(students)                  # 12 obs. of 3 variables, all chr (text)
nrow(students)                 # 12 students

## How many students per city / university?
table(students$city)           # Munich 8, the others 1 each
table(students$university)

## Check with what we know: 8 LMU students in Munich, 12 in total
sum(students$city == "Munich")       # should be 8
length(unique(students$city))        # number of different cities: 5

```

**Task C · Party planning:** Every student brings the drink of their (home) city. How many bottles of each drink do we need? Check your result against what you know about the class.

```{r task_C}
## Look up each student's drink in df_cities (a first "merge" — more in Tutorial 2)
## match() finds, for each student's city, the row of that city in df_cities
students$drink <- df_cities$drink[match(students$city, df_cities$city)]
students                                  # every student now has a drink
table(students$drink)                     # bottles needed per drink

## Check with what we know: 8 LMU students -> should be 8 x Helles beer
sum(students$drink == "Helles beer")      # 8
sum(table(students$drink))                # 12 bottles in total = 12 students
sum(is.na(students$drink))                # 0 = no student without a drink

## Alternative with the same answer (independent implementation)
## merge() joins the two tables by the common column "city"
party_merge <- merge(students, df_cities[, c("city", "drink")], by = "city")
table(party_merge$drink.y)                # same counts as above?
```

# Part 5 · Packages and importing Compustat

**Packages** are collections of functions. Install once per laptop with `install.packages("name")` (or *Tools → Install Packages*), load in every session with `library(name)`. Load all packages at the top of a document. If two packages have functions with the same name, write `package::function()`.

The **tidyverse** is a collection of packages for data analysis: `readr` (import), `dplyr` (manipulation), `ggplot2` (graphics), `tidyr`, `tibble` …

### Chunk 5.1 · Load packages

```{r chunk_5_1}
## install.packages("tidyverse")   # once per laptop, in the Console

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
```

Our data: **Compustat North America**, all public U.S. and Canadian firms, fiscal years 2010–2014 — downloaded from WRDS. Licensed data: it stays in `data/`, it is not pushed to GitHub, and it is not pasted into public AI tools.

| File | Separator | Decimal | Function |
|-----------------|---------------------|-----------------|-------------------|
| `compustat.csv` | `,` | `.` | `read_csv()` (readr) or `read.csv()` (base R) |
| `compustat_German_format.csv` | `;` | `,` | `read_csv2()` or `read.csv2()` |

### Chunk 5.2 · Import the same data three ways

## One-time step, run in the Console: copy the Moodle data from Downloads into data/
## file.copy(from = c("C:/Users/am/Downloads/compustat.csv",
##                    "C:/Users/am/Downloads/compustat_German_format.csv"),
##           to   = here("data"))
## list.files(here("data"))   # check: both files should be listed

```{r chunk_5_2}
## Import the same data three ways

## 1. readr (tidyverse): read_csv() for , separator and . decimals
cs <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"))

## 2. base R: read.csv() - same file, older built-in function
cs_b <- read.csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"))

## 3. readr: read_csv2() for the German format (; separator, , decimals)
cs_g <- read_csv2(here("data", "compustat_German_format.csv"))

## First look: size of each import (rows, columns)
dim(cs)
dim(cs_b)
dim(cs_g)

```

### Chunk 5.3 · Same file, same data? Compare!

```{r chunk_5_3}
## 1. The identifier gvkey
head(cs$gvkey, 2)       # readr:  "001004" "001004"  -> text, zeros kept
head(cs_b$gvkey, 2)     # base R: 1004 1004          -> number, zeros gone!
class(cs$gvkey)         # "character"
class(cs_b$gvkey)       # "integer"

## 2. Type guessing: readr guesses column types from the first 1,000 rows
problems(cs)            # list of cells readr could not read -> set to NA
nrow(problems(cs))      # how many? (slides: 94)

## 3. A safer import: tell R the types instead of letting it guess
cs_safe <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"),
                    col_types = cols(gvkey = "c"),   # gvkey is a code -> character
                    guess_max = Inf)                 # look at ALL rows before guessing types
nrow(problems(cs_safe)) # should be 0 now

## 4. Do the numbers agree across the imports?
sum(cs$at,      na.rm = TRUE)    # total assets, readr
sum(cs_b$at,    na.rm = TRUE)    # base R
sum(cs_g$at,    na.rm = TRUE)    # German format
sum(cs_safe$at, na.rm = TRUE)    # safe import
all.equal(cs_safe$at, cs_g$at)   # TRUE = same values (with tiny tolerance)
```

**Your conclusion:** what differs between the three imports — and which one would you trust? Why?
Conclusion:
- read.csv() drops the leading zeros of gvkey ("001004" -> 1004), so merges would fail.
- read_csv() and read_csv2() keep gvkey, but guess types from the first 1,000 rows and silently set 94 values to NA.
- I trust the safe import: fixed types (gvkey = character) and guess_max = Inf, so nothing is lost.

### Chunk 5.4 · Five checks after every import

```{r chunk_5_4}
## Use the safe import from Chunk 5.3
## 1. Size: rows and columns as expected?
dim(cs_safe)

## 2. Types: numbers numeric, codes text, dates dates?
cs_safe                          # prints first rows + type of each column (<chr>, <dbl>, ...)

## 3. Keys: one row per firm-year?
nrow(cs_safe)                    # number of rows
n_distinct(cs_safe$gvkey, cs_safe$fyear)   # number of unique firm-year combinations
## if these two differ, some firm-years appear more than once (slides: 63,393 vs 57,276)

## 4. Ranges and missing values
summary(cs_safe$at)              # min, max, mean, number of NAs of total assets
sum(cs_safe$at < 0, na.rm = TRUE)   # negative total assets? should be 0
table(cs_safe$fyear)             # all years 2010-2014 present?

## 5. Known value: Apple's total assets, fiscal year 2014 (in USD millions)
## Apple's gvkey is "001690"; the 10-K reports 231,839
filter(cs_safe, gvkey == "001690", fyear == 2014) |>
  select(gvkey, fyear, at, any_of(c("conm", "indfmt", "curcd")))
```

# Part 6 · Coding with AI: bug hunt

The script below was "written by an AI" for the prompt *"Summarise our student cities and the Compustat data."* It looks plausible. Some lines run without any error — and are still wrong.

**Round 1 (10 min, by hand):** Run the chunk. Mark every bug with a comment `# BUG:` and a reason. Use what you know about our cities. **Round 2 (10 min, with AI):** Give the script of chunk 6.1 to an AI tool of your choice (for example the Posit Assistant in RStudio or a chat assistant in the browser) — the code only, **never the Compustat data**: *"Review this R code for bugs. For each bug, explain why it is a bug and how to fix it."* Compare with your list. **Round 3 (5 min):** Which bugs did the AI find that you missed? Which did it miss? Did it invent a bug? What does that mean for how you use AI?

### Chunk 6.1 · The AI-generated script

```{r chunk_6_1, error=TRUE}
## ---- AI-generated script: summary of student cities and Compustat ----

## (a) Number of students per city, added to the city table
n_per_city <- table(students$city)
city_info <- df_cities
city_info$n_students <- c(as.numeric(n_per_city), 0, 0)   # BUG: matches by POSITION, not by name. table() sorts alphabetically (Espoo, Joensuu, Mannheim, Munich, Stockholm), df_cities starts with Munich -> Munich gets 1, Mannheim gets 8. Runs without error, but wrong.
city_info[, c("city", "n_students")]

## (b) Population in millions
city_info$inhabitants_m <- city_info$inhabitants / 1e5    # BUG: 1e5 = 100,000, not a million. Munich shows 15.1 instead of 1.51. Should be 1e6.
city_info[, c("city", "inhabitants_m")]

## (c) German cities only
german <- subset(city_info, country = "Germany")          # BUG: = instead of ==. "=" is read as an (ignored) argument, so nothing is filtered -> 7 rows instead of 2 (Munich, Mannheim). No error, no warning.
nrow(german)

## (d) Average sales of Compustat firms
avg_sales <- mean(cs$sale, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Average sales in thousand USD:", round(avg_sales), "\n")   # BUG: Compustat values are in MILLIONS, not thousands. Also not all USD: Canadian firms report in CAD (curcd), so the mean mixes two currencies.

## (e) Number of firms in the sample
n_firms <- nrow(cs)                                        # BUG: nrow() counts rows = firm-years (plus duplicate rows), not firms. Firms = n_distinct(cs$gvkey).
cat("Number of firms:", n_firms, "\n")

## (f) Median total assets by fiscal year
summarise_median(cs, at, by = fyear)                       # BUG: this function does not exist (AI "hallucination") -> Error: could not find function.
```

### Chunk 6.2 · Solution: bugs, fixes and checks

Write your corrected version below. After every fix, check the result against something you know (e.g., Munich has 8 students).

```{r chunk_6_2}
## (a) match by name, not by position — and check with known values
city_info <- df_cities
city_info$n_students <- as.numeric(n_per_city[city_info$city])   # look up each city BY NAME
city_info$n_students[is.na(city_info$n_students)] <- 0           # Vienna, Shanghai: no home students -> 0
city_info[, c("city", "n_students")]
city_info$n_students[city_info$city == "Munich"]   # check: must be 8
sum(city_info$n_students)                          # check: must be 12

## (b) millions — check: Munich must be about 1.5
city_info$inhabitants_m <- city_info$inhabitants / 1e6
city_info$inhabitants_m[city_info$city == "Munich"]   # check: 1.51

## (c) comparison with == ; check: we know there are exactly two German cities
german <- subset(city_info, country == "Germany")
nrow(german)                                       # check: 2 (Munich, Mannheim)

## (d) units and currency: Compustat items are in millions of the reporting currency
## use the safe import; one format only (indfmt) to avoid double rows; average per currency
cs_safe |>
  filter(indfmt == "INDL") |>
  group_by(curcd) |>
  summarise(avg_sales_millions = mean(sale, na.rm = TRUE), n = n())

## (e) firms vs. firm-years
nrow(cs_safe)                    # rows (firm-years, incl. duplicates)
n_distinct(cs_safe$gvkey)        # number of firms: much smaller

## (f) an existing function — and an independent implementation as check
## Version 1: dplyr
med_dplyr <- cs_safe |>
  group_by(fyear) |>
  summarise(median_at = median(at, na.rm = TRUE))
med_dplyr

## Version 2: base R (independent implementation)
med_base <- tapply(cs_safe$at, cs_safe$fyear, median, na.rm = TRUE)
med_base

## Do both agree?
all.equal(as.numeric(med_base), med_dplyr$median_at)   # TRUE = same result
```
